query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, protective oxide layer above 900 °C are governed by the controlled segregation of the X element at the metal/oxide interface. This segregation modulates the interdiffusional kinetics of cations and enhances stress relaxation, thereby producing a slow-growing, compressively stressed, and adherent oxide scale. In contrast, the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy lacking a targeted X addition forms a rapidly growing, stress-accumulated oxide that cracks or spalls.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (baseline) and CrFeCoNiX variants (with controlled amounts of Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a controlled amount of the fourth element (Si, Mn, or Al) into the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for prolonged durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial compositional gradient arising from the segregation of the X element, which leads to the development of a compressively stressed, coherent oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The added X element preferentially migrates to the metal/oxide interface and reduces the mobility of other cations, thereby slowing the overall oxide growth rate. Simultaneously, it aids in stress relaxation at the interface, resulting in a compressively stressed and adherent oxide layer. Without the X addition, uncontrolled cation diffusion leads to rapid oxide thickening, accumulation of tensile stresses, and subsequent cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with the optimal X addition will exhibit a slower oxide growth rate and form a compressively stressed, coherent, and adherent oxide layer, whereas the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy will develop unstable oxides that crack or spall under similar high-temperature oxidizing/corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with no fourth element (X) addition.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to high-entropy alloys in the single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state under oxidative or corrosive environments at temperatures exceeding 900 °C. The specific beneficial effects are expected only under these elevated temperature conditions and may not hold at lower temperatures or different atmospheric compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of each X element on the rate of interfacial segregation, the exact modification of diffusion kinetics, and the degree of stress relaxation is not yet well established and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy sets: a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy and CrFeCoNiX alloys with controlled additions of Si, Mn, or Al. Subject both sets to oxidation tests in a controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C. Use in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy to monitor elemental segregation at the metal/oxide interface, measure oxide growth kinetics, and assess stress state through appropriate stress measurement techniques.
measurements: Temporal evolution of oxide layer thickness
Measurements of interface and oxide scale stress (e.g., via X-ray diffraction or in-situ stress sensors)
Elemental mapping of the metal/oxide interface (e.g., using APT or STEM-EDS)
Observation and quantification of oxide cracking or spallation events
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrFeCoNiX alloys do not show reduced cation interdiffusion, lack significant segregation of the X element at the interface, or if no appreciable compressive stress and slower oxide growth are observed in comparison to the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. frame.understanding: The hypothesis should focus on how the alloy composition (especially the role of X as Si, Mn, or Al in combination with Cr and other elements) controls the kinetics and structural evolution of the oxide scale. It could posit that specific elemental enrichments at the growth front facilitate a slow-growing, coherent oxide layer by balancing interfacial diffusion and stress relaxation, whereas deviations from this balance lead to rapid oxide growth, internal stresses, cracking, and spallation. Falsification would occur if controlled experiments using the predicted alloy compositions and exposure conditions consistently yield oxide scales that do not demonstrate the expected protective behaviour, or if the expected compositional gradients and diffusion profiles are not observed.

decision.trend: Early studies exploited configurational entropy to stabilize novel oxide phases (PMC4598836) and moved toward long‐term oxidation testing of refractory HEAs, where the formation of protective CrTaO4‐based scales was linked to controlled elemental mixes (PMC6513993). More recently, advanced in‐situ characterizations have been employed to reveal how atomic size effects and redox potentials drive the speciation and evolution of the oxide layer (PMC11169556), yet the interplay between alloying with X = Si, Mn, or Al and the resultant diffusion kinetics and stress relaxation in the oxide remains unquantified. The trend has been to progress from empirical oxidation performance testing to more mechanistic, atom‐scale, in‐situ investigations, but the specific mechanisms by which the X element governs the transition from unstable, spall-prone oxides to slow-growing, coherent scales at high temperature are still unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The fundamental question that remains is how adding a fourth element (Si, Mn, or Al) in CrFeCoNiX specifically tunes the balance between cationic interdiffusion and stress relaxation at the metal/oxide interface above 900 °C, thereby enabling a protective, slow-growing oxide layer instead of rapid growth that leads to cracking/spallation. Neither the compositional gradients nor the stress evolution at the oxide/substrate interface in these alloys have been conclusively linked to the observed failure modes.
decision.lever: Perform a controlled comparison between a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy and variants with targeted X additions (Si, Mn, Al) under oxidation at >900 °C using in-situ characterization (e.g., atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy) coupled with phase-field or atomistic simulation of diffusion and stress evolution at the oxide/metal interface.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend of moving from empirical oxidation tests to mechanistic studies, integrates advanced in-situ techniques with simulation to resolve compositional and stress gradients, and specifically addresses the open question of how the X element alters the kinetics and structure of the protective oxide layer. It provides a testable hypothesis by predicting that optimized X addition will yield a coherent, compressively stressed oxide with slower growth kinetics, whereas deviations will result in unstable, cracking scales.
